artists.biography:
John William Coltrane (also known as "Trane"; September 23, 1926 – July 17, 1967) was an American jazz saxophonist and composer. Working in the bebop and hard bop idioms early in his career, Coltrane helped pioneer the use of modes in jazz and later was at the forefront of free jazz. He organized at least fifty recording sessions as a leader during his recording career, and appeared as a sideman on many other albums, notably with trumpeter Miles Davis and pianist Thelonious Monk.
As his career progressed, Coltrane and his music took on an increasingly spiritual dimension. His second wife was pianist Alice Coltrane and their son Ravi Coltrane is a saxophonist. Coltrane influenced innumerable musicians, and remains one of the most significant saxophonists in jazz history. He received many posthumous awards and recognitions, including canonization by the African Orthodox Church as Saint John William Coltrane. In 2007, Coltrane was awarded the Pulitzer Prize Special Citation for his "masterful improvisation, supreme musicianship and iconic centrality to the history of jazz."

lastfm.wiki_content: Coltrane Plays the Blues is an album by John Coltrane, issued in July 1962 by Atlantic Records (SD 1382). The material was recorded earlier at Atlantic Studios during the sessions that produced My Favorite Things. Recorded in October 1960, the album was compiled and released after Coltrane had ended his association with Atlantic and signed with Impulse Records. As had previously occurred with Prestige, Atlantic drew on unreleased recordings from its archives and issued them without Coltrane’s direct involvement or approval, capitalizing on his rising prominence during the 1960s. Personnel: John Coltrane — soprano & tenor saxophoneMcCoy Tyner — piano (except on Blues to Bechet & Blues to You)Steve Davis — bassElvin Jones — drums Read more on Last.fm. perplexity.description:
Released by Atlantic in 1962, Coltrane Plays the Blues captures John Coltrane in a focused, compact setting drawn from the same 1960 New York sessions that also produced My Favorite Things and Coltrane’s Sound. The album presents six blues-based originals, with Coltrane moving between tenor and soprano saxophones and backed by McCoy Tyner, Steve Davis, and Elvin Jones. Rather than offering straightforward 12-bar templates, the record treats the blues as a flexible expressive language, with driving modal movement, strong melodic hooks, and the telepathic interaction that defined Coltrane’s classic quartet.

The album’s title is apt in spirit if not in strict form: it is less a traditional blues set than a deep exploration of blues feeling within Coltrane’s expanding harmonic world. Pieces such as “Blues to Elvin,” “Blues to Bechet,” and “Mr. Knight” show his ability to turn a familiar idiom into something restless and searching, balancing hard-swinging momentum with lyrical intensity. Long admired as an underrated Atlantic-era album, it has come to be seen as an essential document of Coltrane’s early-1960s transformation, bridging his hard-bop roots and the more adventurous work that followed.
